Emblazon

em-BLAY-zun · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To emblazon to display something prominently on a surface, often by decorating it with a bold design, symbol, or words.

Every fire truck in the county is emblazoned with the department's badge and motto, painted in bright red and gold.

Worked Example

The graduating class voted to emblazon the gymnasium wall with a mural listing every senior's name in gold lettering.

The class wasn't quietly writing names in a corner -- they displayed them boldly and prominently for everyone entering the gym to see.

How Strong Is It? — label → plaster → emblazon

label vs. emblazon

label vs. emblazon: To label something is simply to attach a small identifying tag -- far less bold than a full emblazoned design.

plaster vs. emblazon

plaster vs. emblazon: To plaster a wall with something means covering it all over, an even more overwhelming and inescapable display.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — em-

prefix — em-: to put into a certain state; onto (French/Latin en-)

root — blazon

root — blazon: to display boldly, especially a coat of arms (Old French blason, 'shield')

Put it together

Put it together: Emblazon comes from em- ('onto') + blazon (to boldly display, from the Old French word for a shield) -- literally to put a bold design onto something, the way a coat of arms was once painted onto a knight's shield.

Use the root in a new word: blazon

Use the root in a new word: blazon: On the herald's blazon, a golden lion stood out against a field of deep blue.

Root Check

Word Choice

Emblazon is almost always used for something bold and highly visible -- a flag, a jersey, a banner -- not for small, quiet details. It pairs naturally with the word 'with': something is emblazoned with a design.
